extracted.intended_audience: machine learning / NLP researchers and practitioners working on math word-problem solving, dataset creation, and verification methods for large language models
extracted.subtask_description: Creation, curation, and evaluation of a grade-school math word-problem dataset (GSM8K) and methods for training/verifying language-model solutions via a sample-and-rank verifier pipeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: High Quality (dataset design principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: We avoid error-prone scraping procedures and instead rely on human workers to create problems. After extensive quality control based on workers' answer agreement, we estimate that less than 2 percent of problems contain breaking errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect problems from human contractors; have workers re-solve problems (with no original writer re-solving their own problems); check agreement between solutions and repair/discard disagreements; perform additional rounds of agreement checks (authors report ~1.7% remaining disagreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: High Diversity (dataset design principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: We strive for high diversity among problems and actively avoid designing problems that are drawn from the same linguistic template or differ only in superficial details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create each problem to be relatively unique so held-out test performance is a more relevant metric; compute pairwise similarity scores between problems and provide feedback to contractors to avoid template reuse; allow workers to use GPT-3 seed questions as inspiration but not to re-use templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate Difficulty (dataset design principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a problem distribution challenging for state-of-the-art language models but tractable: problems require 2–8 steps, involve elementary calculations and early-algebra-level concepts, and a bright middle-school student should be able to solve every problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremely hard examples (e.g., MATH-level) and problems that require advanced concepts; ensure most problems can be solved without explicitly defining variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Language Solutions (dataset format requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect solutions in natural language rather than pure math expressions, instructing problem writers to explain their work as much as possible while allowing diverse linguistic styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural language solutions enable interpretability and help probe models' internal monologues; prefer explanation-rich responses over terse equation-only answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label correctness by final answer (verifier/generator labeling rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Training solutions are labeled correct or incorrect solely based on whether they reach the correct final answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware this labeling yields false positives where the final numeric answer is correct despite flawed reasoning; these false positives are an accepted limitation of this labeling scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample-and-rank verification pipeline
rubrics_metrics.description: At test time, sample many candidate solutions from a generator and select the one ranked highest by a verifier which outputs a probability that a candidate solution is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train a generator (finetuned LM) to produce diverse completions, sample (e.g., 100) high-temperature solutions, score with a verifier, and return the highest-scoring solution; training verifier on generator outputs improves performance compared to baseline finetuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit generator finetuning to preserve coverage (recommended: 2 epochs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train the generator only for a small number of epochs (authors use 2) to retain coverage/diversity of generated solutions; longer finetuning leads to overconfidence and collapse in diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor test@N behavior: test@1 may improve with more epochs but test@100 (coverage) can degrade sharply; select generator checkpoints that maximize coverage for verifier training (authors use 2 epochs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test@N evaluation metric (test solve rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use test@N = percentage of problems solved correctly at least once when allowing N separate guesses per problem. Test performance is measured by checking whether the final answer matches the correct answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report test@1 for single low-temperature samples and test@100 for multi-sample/verification settings; present means and standard deviations across multiple runs where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling temperature choices for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use low temperature (T = 0) to generate deterministic test@1 samples and higher temperature (T = 0.7) to generate diverse samples for test@100/verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperatures were chosen empirically; alternatives (e.g., T=1.0) had negligible effect in ablations, but T=0 for single-sample evaluation and ~0.7 for multi-sample search worked well in the authors' experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token-level verifier vs solution-level verifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifiers can predict correctness after each token (token-level) or only after the final token (solution-level); token-level verifiers act like a per-token value function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Token-level verifiers are more challenging/noisy to train but ultimately outperform solution-level verifiers and are less prone to overfitting; token-level predictions also provide an interpretable, fine-grained signal across a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint verifier objective (verification + language modeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train the verifier with a joint objective: the verification loss (predict correctness) plus a standard language modeling objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including the language modeling objective is a strict improvement versus verification-only objectives; implement by mixing language data and verifier-labeled data in training (authors mix equally, effectively upsampling language data when many verifier examples exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual dropout regularization (use dropout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply residual dropout (authors use 20%) during finetuning and verifier training to reduce overfitting and improve performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because GPT-3 pretraining did not use dropout, perform additional pretraining with dropout before finetuning to mitigate distribution shift; dropout significantly improves finetuning baseline and helps solution-level verifiers avoid overfitting; token-level verifiers also gain slightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculator annotations to mitigate arithmetic errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Inject calculation annotations into training so models can call a calculator; at test time, override sampling when a well-formatted annotation exists to evaluate the expression and insert the numeric result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotations were auto-generated by a mix of hard-coded logic and a finetuned LM; simulate calculator by evaluating expressions (authors used python eval); imperfect annotation logic may ignore some lines but rarely generates incorrect annotations; fixing minor calculator bugs improved reported test performance by ~1%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate generator and verifier models (to avoid overfitting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train separate networks for generator and verifier to limit generator training and prevent overfitting and collapse of diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although in principle combination is possible, authors found better empirical results initializing the verifier from the generator checkpoint but keeping them as distinct models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining number of completions at test time (compute-vs-performance tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test-time performance depends on how many completions are sampled and scored: performance typically improves up to some point and then can degrade due to adversarial solutions that fool the verifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors observe improvement up to ~400 completions for a 6B model, with decrease beyond; they use 100 completions as a practical tradeoff capturing most benefits with modest compute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority-vote among top-ranked solutions (voting scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of selecting only the single top-ranked solution, take a majority vote among the final answers of the top-K verifier-ranked solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimal K depends on the total number of samples: for 100 samples allow ~3–5 top samples to vote; for 3200 samples allow ~30 top samples; votes consider only the final numeric answer, not full reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifier training dataset generation (100 completions per training example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate many (authors use 100) completions from the generator for each training problem, label each completion correct/incorrect by final answer, and train the verifier on this dataset (authors train verifier for 1 epoch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using many completions per training example provides a rich negative set and enables the joint objective (LM+verifier). When mixing LM and verifier data equally, this procedure effectively up-samples original LM data by the number of completions per problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifier architecture and prediction head
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement the verifier as a language model with a small scalar head that outputs predictions on a per-token basis by shifting and scaling the logit for a special token (using a bias and gain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lets the LM logits continue to represent the language modeling objective while a reserved special token is used for verification predictions; initialize verifier from generator checkpoint for slightly better performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criterion: final answer correctness (finite, deterministic check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both finetuning baseline and verification success are measured by whether the returned solution's final answer equals the ground-truth final answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finetuning, generating intermediate natural-language steps is crucial: training a finetuned model to directly output only the final answer drastically reduces performance (authors report drop from 20.6% to 5.2% for a 6B model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model size impacts: generator size matters more than verifier size
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing generator size yields larger gains than increasing verifier size; having a large generator with a small verifier outperforms a small generator with a large verifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests verifiers rely on coarse heuristics to discriminate solutions from a given generator; verification nevertheless remains effective even when the verifier is much smaller than the generator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperparameter choices used as practical recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors report specific hyperparameters that work well: batch size ~3.2e4 tokens, max sample length 400 tokens, Adam optimizer with β1=0.9, β2=0.95, residual dropout default 0.0 (0.2 for dropout experiments), learning rate schedules, finetuning epochs=20 (but 2 for generator when producing samples for verification), verifier epochs=1, verifier loss=MSE, completions per train/test problem=100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors swept learning rate and batch size by orders of magnitude and found no significant improvements; for verification they recommend generator trained 2 epochs to produce diverse samples, sampling temperature 0.7 when generating many completions, and using 100 completions at train and test time as a practical default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control measures for data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple rounds of human agreement checks, re-solving by independent workers, and compute similarity metrics to prevent template reuse; allow workers to use GPT-3 generated seeds but require explanation-rich solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discard or repair problems with disagreement; estimate residual error rate (authors report ~1.7% disagreements after QC) and be transparent about possible subtle remaining errors.
